These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish. This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS survey team concluded an EF-0 tornado produced damage to trees, several homes, and several electrical wooden poles in the McCord area of Houma. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak winds near 95 mph touched down west of Loda with initial damage consisting of the collapse of two empty grain bins. The tornado continued ENE crossing into Iroquois County southwest of Buckley, downing and uprooting trees and blowing over semi-trucks on Interstate 57. Near the end of the damage track, the roof of a large outbuilding was removed, while nearby trees were snapped near the base and deposited in various directions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms brought intense storms to the region during the late evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The storms delivered a severe combination of damaging wind gusts, large hail, and an isolated tornado. Moving through the state in the overnight hours, a line of storms impacted Jasper and Newton counties with heavy rain, wind, and lightning. Early morning video documented significant tree damage and downed power lines near 1st and Schifferdecker in Joplin. Widespread wind damage tore the roof off the Joplin Parks and Recreation building and leveled several metal outbuildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service survey concluded an EF1 tornado with peak winds of 95mph damaged an outdoor maintenance storage building at the golf course at the W 2nd Street and S Schifferdecker Ave in Joplin. The tornado then tracked to the northeast downing numerous trees in a cyclonic manner. Minor roof damage occurred to a few homes, and several other homes were damaged by trees falling on them.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms, a tornado and flash flooding occurred during the evening of June 21, lasting into the morning of June 22.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS ground survey along with public reports determined that an EF0 tornado with a 200 yard wide path initially touched down in a wooded area at the end of County Road H-522 to the southeast of Eminence. The tornado damaged a barn then both broke and uprooted trees as it crossed Highway H and along Highway NN to the Rocky Falls Shut In area off County Road NN-526.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the evening of June 10th.  Scattered wind damage was observed along and north of the I-72 corridor, with the most concentrated damage focusing across portions of Menard, Logan, Sangamon, and Macon counties where the cells interacted with an existing outflow boundary from earlier storms.  Six tornadoes touched down within this corridor, including an EF-1 tornado that tracked across Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport and the north side of Springfield.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down along Moore Road about 3 miles west of Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport at 11:04pm CDT.  It tracked eastward across the airport, lofting 6,000lb aircraft hangars and rolling an enclosed trailer.  The tornado then struck the Animal Protective League animal shelter on Taintor Road where it uplifted the roof and collapsed the east wall of the building.  As it continued across the north side of Springfield, numerous trees were damaged or snapped and a few homes sustained siding and shingle damage.  The tornado then moved across Camp Butler and into Mechanicsburg where it caused additional tree and building damage before dissipating about 5 miles east of Mechanicsburg just north of the Sangamon River at 11:30pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in an environment favorable for organized updrafts. Although the majority of the activity stayed well to the south of Adams County, one cell did pass through the area where it produced a brief tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 26th, near a warm front as an upper level disturbance approached the region from the west. The atmosphere across eastern Oklahoma became very unstable during the afternoon and early evening and the deep-layer wind shear was strong with the approach of the upper level disturbance. Some of the thunderstorms were able to develop into supercells due to the favorable combination of instability and wind shear. Several tornadoes and large hail up to quarter size occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado was observed by several storm chasers. It remained over open country with no known damage. The path details were based on the storm chaser observations and radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous low-pressure system and cold front pushed through the Plains and the Ozarks, interacting with a warm, moist air mass as a strong upper-level trough and a veered wind profile created high wind shear and instability. This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.

The tornado flipped several mobile homes resting on blocks, damaged signs and roofing associated with stores along Highway 65, and created a pattern of tree damage including many uprooted or snapped, surveyed through in-person and Sentinel-2 satellite surveys. The tornado tracked for a little over 6 miles with a path width of 200 yards and maximum wind speeds of 90mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video and photo evidence of a small tornado near this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Oklahoma on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across southeastern Oklahoma and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the area was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. A tornado, isolated damaging wind, and large hail up to two inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed west of the 4240 Road, near Pinekke Road. It moved east-southeast snapping large tree limbs and uprooting small trees. The tornado crossed Highway 93 on the northern banks of Lake Hugo, where some trees were uprooted and large tree limbs were snapped. Numerous trees were uprooted and a few were snapped south of Apple, and a home was damaged. It continued to move east-southeast across the E2000 Road, and then crossed Highway 147 before dissipating over rugged terrain. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

The thunderstorms organized into a squall line and moved eastward into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 15th. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is the second segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado crossed into Washington County, AR, near the 4765 Road. It crossed the Baron Fork River, and damaged outbuildings, uprooted trees, and snapped numerous large tree limbs along Salem Springs Road. Trees were uprooted or snapped along Highway 59 and Sugar Hill Road, before the tornado dissipated southwest of Lincoln. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 30, 2026, an oppressive tropical airmass fueled by extreme heat warnings collided with a sharp mid-level shortwave across the NWS Buffalo CWA, prompting the Storm Prediction Center to issue a Severe Thunderstorm Watch as strong boundary-layer destabilization produced widespread severe convection across Central New York and the North Country. NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions highlighted surging moisture and extreme instability that unleashed powerful multi-cell clusters and isolated supercells, leading to severe straight-line microbursts with winds up to 100 mph and an EF-1 tornado touchdown in Lewis County. Concurrently, deep warm-cloud processes and precipitable water levels approaching 2.0 inches fueled torrential precipitation efficiency, driving Weather Prediction Center Excessive Rainfall concerns for localized flash flooding in poor-drainage areas. As the pre-frontal convective line swept east toward nightfall, loss of daytime heating and post-frontal drying rapidly stabilized the region, bringing an end to the severe weather threat into the overnight hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northwest Pennsylvania. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief tornado touched down in central Crawford County near Leimbach Road at approximately 4:29 PM EDT. The tornado touched down west of Leimbach Road and north of Double Hill Road, then moved generally east-southeast. Damage consisted primarily of snapped and uprooted trees. Several trees were snapped near the point of touchdown, and a falling tree clipped and damaged a well-constructed detached garage. As the tornado crossed Leimbach Road, several large hardwood trees were uprooted. The fallen trees were oriented toward the northeast, consistent with the localized tornadic wind field despite the tornado's overall east-southeast movement. Based on the observed damage, maximum wind speeds were estimated at 95 mph, yielding an EF-1 tornado rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards and produced a short, intermittent damage path before dissipating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief EF-0 tornado dropped from locally lower ceilings within a bookend vortex embedded in the QLCS near Cecil Harden Lake, 1.3 miles southeast of the Hollandsburg community.  The bookend vortex crossed the lake, spawning the weak spin-up one-quarter mile south of the lake's southeastern shoreline;  along its 900-foot track, the tornado then crossed residential roads East Mallard Drive and South Ebert Drive, before ending 400 feet south of the lake's shore.||Drone imagery showed clear convergence of downed trees in a grove between Meadows Lane and Mallard Drive;  30 to 40 additional trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path.  Incident structural damage was limited to minor siding loss.  The tornado's damage was mainly vegetation, with peak ind gusts of 85 mph for the event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado touched down in northern Poinsett County early in the morning on Tuesday, April 28. The tornado occurred over an open field and no damage was reported. Since no damage indicators were found, this tornado is rated an EF-Unknown.

Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several videos and photographs from multiple angles indicated that a weak tornado developed and moved to the east northeast along this approximate path. While the near-surface dust cloud was wider, the core circulation was quite narrow and weak. The only damage along the track was minor tree damage as it crossed mostly open fields. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Enid Tornado initially developed near or on the southwest portion of Vance Air Force Base and moved east-northeast crossing over the southern edge of the runway complex, but remaining south of the majority of structures on the base. However as the tornado crossed US-81, it moved through the Gray Ridge Estates neighborhood where most of the houses in the neighborhood sustained damage, and many destroyed or receiving significant damage. Damage to at least three homes in this neighborhood was rated EF4. ||After moving northeast out of this neighborhood, the tornado moved through open land. Although the tornado continued moving through areas without structures, damage done to trees east of Leona Mitchell Blvd and north of Fox Drive was significant. At least one tree was debarked, and a hardwood tree was pulled from the ground and displaced 20 feet to the east. Farther northeast, significant ground scouring and severe tree damage was observed as the tornado crossed E0455 Road and South 16th Street. At Southgate Road, a number of structures were destroyed including two metal buildings, a warehouse and an outbuilding. An RV parked in this area was picked up and the chassis of this RV was found about 305-310 yards northeast of its origination point. Damage was rated EF4 in this area as well.||The tornado moved through more open land damaging trees as it approached S 30th Street. Radar and damage patterns indicate that the tornado moved in a loop briefly just southwest of South 30th Street and Rupe Road. A home was destroyed (EF4) and a number of other structures and trees were destroyed or heavily damaged along South 30th Street. Coming out of the loop, the tornado moved southeast across S 30th Street thereby continuing in relatively open land as opposed to moving northeast toward a d neighborhood on the southeast side of Enid. A farmstead was hit at S 42nd Street and Rupe Road destroying a barn, damaging the house and trees on the property.||Crossing Rupe Road, radar indicated the tornado likely moved in a loop again northeast of Rupe Road and S 42nd Street, before moving southeast and east and dissipating near Boggy Creek just west of Woodring Airport.||Despite the intensity of this tornado, there was only one injury that required transport.||Scientific notes: Researchers at the National Severe Storms Laboratory and the University of Illinois performed a variety of calculations to estimate the potential wind speed of the tornado. Two researchers performed a treefall pattern analysis to match the observed pattern of treefall to a simulated pattern from a vortex model. One researcher used this method to determine a probabilistic wind speed distribution from treefall near Southgate Road using six different sets of constraints. The calculated median maximum 3-second velocity in all of these six experiments was over 205 mph, and the interquartile range of two of these six experiments was completely over 200 mph. ||A second researcher also performed a treefall analysis with a Monte Carlo simulation slightly adjusting the input variables. Taking the runs with the lowest 0.5% error, a median estimated maximum wind velocity of 94 m/s (210 mph) was calculated.||A third researcher made calculations of the 300 yard displacement of the RV near Southgate Road using simulations with a 3-dimensional vortex model that does include modeled vertical motion of the tornado, again using a Monte Carlo simulation. Of the simulations that provided the closest match the displacement of the RV, the maximum winds of these simulations were 91-97 m/s (204-217 mph).||Based on these engineering calculations that included both 3-dimensional vortex modeling (including vertical motions) and 3-second averaging wind speed averaging consistent with the EF-scale values, it is very highly likely that this tornado produced winds that would be classified as an EF5 tornado in the vicinity of Southgate Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 26th, near a warm front as an upper level disturbance approached the region from the west. The atmosphere across eastern Oklahoma became very unstable during the afternoon and early evening and the deep-layer wind shear was strong with the approach of the upper level disturbance. Some of the thunderstorms were able to develop into supercells due to the favorable combination of instability and wind shear. Several tornadoes and large hail up to quarter size occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado was witnessed by numerous storm chasers and remained over mainly open country. Power poles were snapped by the tornado on Foraker Road, south of Foraker. Otherwise, no known damage occurred from this tornado. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 85 to 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began in far eastern Whiteside County just north of Fulfs Road and just west of the Whiteside-Lee county line, where satellite imagery showed the beginning of a narrow southwest-northeast path of disturbed soil through farm fields. Drone footage taken along Mound Hill Road in Lee County revealed swirl marks in the field to the west that aligned with the path that was evident in the satellite imagery, confirming that the tornado remained on the ground continuously as it tracked into Lee County. The tornado crossed Mound Hill Road, downing a number of power poles and impacting a property on the east side of the road. The tornado reached its peak intensity here, destroying multiple outbuildings and snapping several trees at this property. The tornado left additional swirl marks in a field to the northeast of the property before causing damage to trees, a residence, and a metal outbuilding along and just south of Lenox Road. As the tornado reached Timber Creek Road, it caused damage to a barn, at least one power pole, and several trees. On the north side of the road, the tornado pushed an old barn off of its foundation into a grain leg, causing the grain leg to collapse. A concrete silo was also toppled at the same location. The tornado then continued northeastward, causing tree and roof damage at a property along Peek Home Road, then damaging an outbuilding, a house, and more trees at a property at Penrose Road and Swarts Road. The tornado produced its last instance of damage at the Hey Tree Service facility along U.S. Route 52/State Route 26 southeast of Woosung before dissipating prior to reaching the Ogle County line. Straight-line wind damage was also observed to the south and east of the tornado's track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.

The tornado also caused minor tree damage along CR 328, lifting after crossing Highway 139. This survey was assisted by law enforcement camera footage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is the second segment of a three-segment tornado. The tornado moved into Adair County south of the 754 Road, and into rugged terrain. Trees were uprooted as it moved across the 4630 Roads southwest of Christie, and the roof of a manufactured home was damaged. The tornado uprooted numerous trees and snapped numerous large tree limbs along Highway 62, with more trees uprooted along Cemetery Road and Highway 59, and along the 4750 Road before moving into Washington County, AR. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 90 to 100 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite considerable cloud cover across East Texas ahead of a cold front, relatively modest surface heating was ongoing by late morning on April 4th. A very moist air mass characterized by dew points in the upper 60s to lower 70s preceded the front. This environment supported scattered thunderstorm development along and ahead of the cold front, further aided by being on the southern fringe of the stronger mid-level winds helping propel the front. Additionally, MLCAPE values increasing to 1500+ J/kg and 25-35 knots of effective shear supported marginally organized storms capable of wind damage, flash flooding, and isolated tornadoes. However, poor mid-level lapse rates and a linear mode limited hail potential. As a result, one severe thunderstorm with quasi-supercell structure produced a brief tornado near Lindale in Smith County while a separate cluster of thunderstorms led to isolated flash flooding in Longview in Gregg County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mini-supercell developed and produced a short-lived, small, but intense EF1 tornado east and northeast of Lindale, TX. The tornado began in a field just south of FM Road 16 West, downing some small tree limbs and snapping the trunk of a pecan tree. At this same location, significant roof damage, consisting of shingle and roof decking loss, occurred to a single-family residence, resulting in a rating of EF1. The tornado downed a few more tree limbs before crossing FM Road 16 West. A couple of homes in the Woodcrest subdivision sustained minor shingle damage. Home security cameras in this|subdivision recorded the tornado's passage. The tornado continued northeast and crossed Legion Hills Road. In this location, a second single-family home sustained significant roof damage corresponding to a rating of EF1. A large oak tree was also uprooted on this property. The tornado continued northeast sporadically downing large tree limbs. A few more tree limbs were downed before the tornado lifted near the intersection of FM Road 2710 and County Road 4107. The tornado had estimated maximum wind speeds of 97 mph, a path length of approximately 2.5 miles, and a path width of 32 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed a little less than one mile north of Webb just east of 290th Avenue in an open field.  The tornado was documented by numerous individuals as it tracked east-northeast for a little over a minute. The tornado crossed 300th Avenue near a farmstead where trees were damaged along the north side of the property and the resultant winds caused minor damage to the residence.  The tornado continued toward the east-northeast for a little over a minute over open fields and lifted just before 310th Avenue south of 470th Street. The tornado was rated EF0 with a maximum estimated wind speed of 75 mph. The average path width was 30 yards.

Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. The tornado tracked across Mount Hope Dairy, destroying one barn and damaging another before quickly lifting. Debris from the barns was scattered north of 290th Street in a southwest to northeast orientation. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois and West Kentucky compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri.||In Northwest Kentucky, during the late evening, MLCAPE remained elevated ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 1000-2000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-6, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C.||Reports from West Kentucky primarily came from an intensifying line of storms entering the Western Coal Fields area from the northwest. A swath of straight-line winds accompanied the first tornadic circulation. The tornadoes damaged numerous trees, some electrical lines and power poles, and a few homes and outbuildings. Several other straight-line wind damage reports were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. Peak winds were 85 mph.

As the storms progressed eastward through the evening, they moved into a favorable environment for tornado and severe wind development. Several tornadoes were observed across northeast Iowa, southeast South Dakota, and extreme southern Minnesota. There were two tornadoes in Freeborn County and one tornado in Martin County.||In addition to the tornadoes, there were reports of wind damage across southern MN. Minor structural damage and scattered tree damage suggest wind speeds around 60 to 75 mph were likely tied to the thunderstorms.

Likely a QLCS tornado that developed in a field just east of US HWY 65, crossing 810th Ave and damaging several trees and a few buildings before it dissipated just south of 130th Street between Glenville and Gordonsville, MN. The maximum wind speed was estimated at 90 mph.

This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado touched down just north of U.S. Highway 278 and west of Holly Pond near the intersection of County Roads 1650 and 1682. There, it quickly assumed EF1 status, uprooting a hardwood tree, and causing door damage to small farm outbuildings nearby.  The tornado tracked generally northeastward, uprooting and snapping large hardwood trees along County Road 1683. Farther northeast, near the intersection of County Roads 1709, 1710, and 1711, multiple hardwood trees were snapped and uprooted, and in a small neighborhood there, a house experienced roof damage.  The tornado continued to track generally northeastward across a mix of open farmland and woodland, with snapped and uprooted hardwood trees again observed along County Road 1716.  To the northeast in the Brooklyn community, the tornado uprooted and snapped hardwood trees along County Road 1684, and minor roof damage occurred to a single family dwelling. There were also two cattle deaths due to tree falls off of County Road 1684. The tornado crossed northward on the east side of Brooklyn, and headed farther northeast to the east side of Baileyton, where it occasionally snapped and uprooted hardwood trees along the way.  Just to the northeast of Baileyton along County Road 1762, the tornado caused tree damage, with one large tree falling on and damaging a truck. Roof damage also occurred to a nearby house.  Farther northeast along County Road 1763, the tornado uprooted hardwood and softwood trees, pushed a mobile home off its foundation, and caused significant roof damage to the dwelling.  The tornado began curving slightly westward as it neared the intersections of Highway 67 and 69, causing sporadic tree damage along the way and also along Apple Grove Road. The tornado then tracked north-northwestward, ending on County Road 1589 just west of Highway 67.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several slow-moving thunderstorms developed across the southern Nebraska Panhandle and northern Nebraska Panhandle, bringing hail, tornadoes, and torrential rain fall with flooding occuring in Kimball and Dawes Counties. No verification occurred in southeast Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kimball County EM reported an ongoing tornado with a ground circulation of dust. This was originally reported as debris, but later an Emergency Manager confirmed no damage. Therefore, this tornado was rated an EF-U.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado briefly touched down near Parrish in Manatee County as a developing thunderstorm interacted with intersecting sea breeze and convective outflow boundaries resulting in a brief spin-up. Elsewhere, easterly sea breeze afternoon convection produced a severe wind gust near Punta Gorda in Charlotte County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado briefly touched down just west of U.S. Hwy 301, where the resident of a home along Loch Ness Gln witnessed damage to the backyard fence. The resident reported that the tornado lifted shortly thereafter, while another area resident witnessed debris being lofted in an open field just to the north prior to the tornado lifting. No additional damage or reports were received.

The tornado was estimated to touch down north of U.S. Highway 18 east of 458th Avenue and tracked northeast for less than a minute before it lifted just west of 459th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 20 yards based on video evidence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough moved across a dryline northwest of South-Central Texas and generated thunderstorms that moved into our area. Storm motion was toward the east-northeast while the low-level flow was from the southeast. This vertical wind shear in one of the storms was enough to produce a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service determined an EF-0 tornado touched down in Lee County this morning based on photos and drone footage received by the Lee County office of emergency management, combined with radar analysis. The tornado formed roughly six miles southwest of Giddings, roughly near the CR 208 and FM 2239, and moved northeast into Giddings before dissipating. Sporadic damage was observed to power lines, tree limbs, and tin sheds, as well as some small sections of tin roofs and eaves peeled back. Peak winds of 70 mph were estimated.

As it traveled a winding path generally eastward, extensive tree damage occurred along the path, including snapped tree trunks and uprooted trees. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few severe thunderstorms produced large hail across the Concho Valley and Northern Edwards Plateau. Also, a lightning strike destroyed a hotel in Brady.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a brief tornado touchdown reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak wave of low pressure along a stationary front resulted in strong to severe thunderstorms tracking east across southern WI during the late evening and overnight  hours.  A tornado was documented in far southwest Wisconsin with other tree damage noted due to high winds.

Along Penny Benton Rd, it hit 6 trees, 1 uprooted, 1 snapped at the trunk but was rotted.  As it tracked east, it hit some metal farm buildings along Mullen Rd and south of Copeland Rd.  Corn stubble from the field to the west was noted deposited along the farm driveway with sheet metal from the barns lofted up the hill and into the forest to the east.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough moved through northern Arizona generating a few showers and thunderstorms.  One of the storms produced a landspout tornado in Apache County in eastern Arizona.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A developing thunderstorm over Tampa Bay produced a brief EF-0 tornado that affected the Villages of Bayport community in Hillsborough County.  Elsewhere, easterly sea breeze afternoon convection produced a funnel cloud near Buckingham in Lee County.

Residents in the neighborhood reported and shared images of a few additional structures that sustained minor damage. Additionally, a large tree was also blown over in the community one street over from where the main damage was noted. No additional damage or reports could be located.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 Tornado with a path length of 3.71 miles and path width of 100 yards moved through this area. The estimated peak winds were 105 mph with damage including snapped trees and two barns destroyed. The tornado touched down just east of Co Road 300E where multiple trees were snapped about 15 to 20 ft above ground. The tornado then moved northeast and caused substantial damage to barns and to at least one home across a three to four mile path before lifting near Co Road 600E to the north of County Road 1000N. The tornado may not have been on the ground continuously for the whole track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began in rural far eastern Vernon County where it caused minor damage to a residence and damaged some trees before moving into Juneau County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the late evening of April 17th producing scattered wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A narrow EF-1 tornado touched down near the intersection of W 1700 S and S 350 W roads near Kentland, where several large tree branches were downed. The tornado then crossed US Highway 41 at peak intensity, downing a billboard, uplifting a large portion of the roof of a restaurant, and pushing over a semi truck. A farm outbuilding was damaged nearby, as well. Debris was thrown nearly 2 miles downstream in an open field just north of US Highway 24. A narrow path evident in satellite imagery in open fields to the northeast of this debris suggested that the tornado likely continued to the northeast for approximately two more miles without impacting any trees or structures before dissipating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very warm temperatures led to a well-mixed lower atmosphere. Weak winds and a weakly convergence boundary in the presence of marginal moisture led to the development of high-based convection, which featured a widely viewed landspout that drifted west-southwest from Minnesota into South Dakota.

The highly visible tornado was viewed from numerous angles as it traversed slowly across open fields to the west-southwest.  The tornado crossed the state line out of Rock County one-half mile south of 41st Street on 488th Avenue. The landspout continued west-southwest through Minnehaha County for less than one mile before it dissipated at 1626CST. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating in either Rock County or Minnehaha County, giving the tornado a rating of EFU in both counties. The average path width was estimated at 40 yards based on video and photo evidence.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several videos were shared of a slow-moving landspout tornado that occurred a few miles east of Beaverville and north northeast of Donovan in rural northeast Iroquois County. No known damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the late evening of April 17th producing scattered wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began just west of the Illinois-Indiana state line near CR 9000N in northeast Kankakee County. The first instances of damage included uprooted softwood trees, downed large branches from hardwood trees, and minor structural damage noted near Stateline Rd on either side of the border. As the tornado quickly tracked northeast, it caused additional tree damage on at least one property near US-41. Along the path toward and through Lowell, the tornado blew out sections of a gas station canopy along IN-2 and then a garage wall at a residence just northwest of downtown Lowell. This was in addition to causing further tree and minor structural damage in a defined narrow path. The tornado  continued through southern and southeastern sections of Lake Dalecarlia, causing primarily tree damage and minor structural damage due to fallen trees. Based on the ground survey, the tornado likely dissipated prior to reaching IN-55.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado formed west of US Highway 148 at its intersection with Puddin Valley Road, in northern Jack County. This tornado tracked southeastward through open country, producing scattered tree damage and light structural damage to one residence. The tornado dissipated shortly after crossing Post Oak Road. The damage was consistent with high-end EF-0 windspeeds of 75-80 mph.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-2 tornado occurred on the southwest side of Runaway Bay with peak winds estimated at 130 mph. This tornado formed just south of Highway 380 near Port O Call Drive and Pinto Court where a 100 to 200 yard wide swath of EF-0 tree damage was observed. The tornado then continued towards the west, uprooting some trees and snapping large branches as it approached Cimmarron Trail. By this time the tornado was nearly a third of a mile wide, causing substantial tree damage and minor roof damage before moving into a residential area between Cimmarron Trail and Jasper Creek Road. Most homes in this neighborhood sustained high-end EF-0 and EF-1 damage with heavily damaged manufactured homes, broken windows, failed garage doors, uprooted trees, and substantial roof damage to single family homes. Within the broader area of EF-0/EF-1 damage, small vortices embedded in the tornado produced narrow corridors of EF-2 damage. The first instance was a two-floor residence on the northeast corner of the Cactus Canyon Drive and Brookview Drive intersection. Here, the home lost a substantial amount of roofing along with some exterior walls on the second floor. Two single-wide manufactured homes in the vicinity of this house were completely destroyed with debris displaced away from their original location. A second home in the northeast side of the neighborhood on Cactus Canyon Drive lost nearly all of its roofing. Wind estimates of this damage ranged from 120-125 mph. The most intense damage was observed with a double-wide manufactured home near the intersection of Overland Trail and Cumberland Trail. The metal frame was found 100 yards downwind of the original home site, with additional debris several hundred yards to the west. Severe tree damage was also noted just on the west side of Jasper Creek Road. This damage was consistent with a high-end EF-2 intensity tornado containing estimated wind speeds of up to 130 mph. A fatality occurred in this destroyed residence. The tornado was also at its peak width during this time, just over half a mile wide. The tornado continued into a forested area dissipating approximately 600 yards west of Jasper Creek Road, completing its 1.4 mile long path.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A high-end EF-1 tornado began near Meridian Road between Favor Road and Steward Road southeast of Harrison, initially causing damage to trees and an outbuilding. Video footage from storm chasers documented the tornado becoming fully condensed and growing in size and intensity as it tracked east-northeastward across Favor Road and impacted two farmsteads, causing significant damage to a few outbuildings and snapping and uprooting multiple trees. Additional storm chaser footage showed the tornado intensifying again as it tracked northeastward across Gummow Road and then reaching peak intensity as it impacted a property along Freeport Road. At this property, the majority of an older two-story house's roof was removed, several trees were snapped, and an old barn was destroyed. The footage then captured the tornado making a sharp turn to the southeast and crossing Freeport Road once again before roping out and eventually dissipating in open fields near Owen Center Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado formed near the intersection of Spring Valley Road and Wise County Road 3355.  This tornado initially moved south, producing scattered tree, shingle, and outbuilding roof damage consistent with high end EF-0 winds.  The tornado crossed FM 2123, just east of its intersection with Wise County Road 3355 in the Cottondale community, and dissipated shortly thereafter.  Maximum estimated winds were 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado appeared to touch down in an open field southwest of the intersection of E 1200 North Road and N 2450 East Road and impacted a farm, leading to damage to several structures. The tornado then continued northeastward, causing damage to trees and farm outbuildings. The peak intensity of the tornado occurred near the end of the path along the Iroquois and Newton County border, where over a dozen new wooden power poles were snapped at their base. The tornado then appeared to lift just northeast of US-24 in southwestern Newton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An eyewitness observed a tornado develop 2 miles northeast of Archer south of 350th Street in an open field. The tornado tracked northwest slowly over the next five minutes through open fields. After crossing Pierce Avenue, the tornado dissipated. There was no known damage, resulting in an EFU rating. The location, track, and a maximum path width of 25 yards was estimated from video.

This second tornado formed west of Post Oak Road, just north of its intersection with Campsey Road. The tornado moved southeast in open terrain producing substantial tree damage as it paralleled Campsey Road. Most of these trees exhibited damage consistent with high-end EF-0 winds on the order of 70-80 mph. However, a number of trees exhibited more significant snapping and twisting along this part of the track, commensurate with low end EF-1 wind speeds of approximately 90 mph. The tornado continued southeast for approximately 4-5 more miles producing additional high end EF-0 and low end EF-1 damage to trees, a couple of oil storage tanks, and a few homes and outbuildings. The tornado crossed State Highway 59 west of Cundiff, continued to track southeast and dissipated before reaching Coca Cola Ranch Road near the West Fork of the Trinity River.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began near Junction Lane and Ard Trail in far southeastern Lincoln County, crossing Holmesville Road as it moved into far southwestern Lawrence County around Homesville Road. It continued across Woody Road, WS Cothern Road, and MS Highway 44, passing near the center of the Jayess community. It then tracked across Jessie Wallace Road and Latrell Sanders Road before lifting just north of the Walthall County line. Along the path, numerous trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths. Utility poles were leaning or broken with several lines downed. Multiple homes and outbuildings sustained roof and siding damage, and a business received roof damage. A poultry farm southeast of Jayess sustained roof damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 110 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly advancing cold front was positioned beneath strong west-southwesterly flow downstream of a broad upper-level trough with embedded shortwaves. A moist low level layer and strong instability combined with strengthening deep-layer and low-level wind shear to support discrete supercells across southwest and southern Mississippi during the late afternoon and evening. These storms produced large hail and multiple tornadoes over southwest Mississippi, one EF1 and one EF2 tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This summary covers primarily the Wilkinson County, MS portion of the track. For more information regarding this tornado please refer to WFO Jackson, MS's public information statements. The damage path of a large and significant tornado began between E Sibley Farms Rd and US Hwy 61 in Adams County, MS. Gray Sky/Vexcel and Sentinel-2 high-resolution satellite imagery was heavily leveraged over this rural and inaccessible portion of the track. The tornado produced occasional swaths of defined EF-1 tree damage as it moved into Wilkinson County along the Homochitto River and the damage path became apparently much larger and more multi-vortex in nature with several swaths of damage noted from vortices along and south of the mean path. The sheer amount of tree damage that extended over a half mile south of the mean track made it difficult to differentiate between RFD and subtornadic vortex damage, but the ingestion of this vorticity clearly assisted in rapid intensification of this tornado beyond Possum Corner, MS. An increasingly intense and large swath of downed trees began near Possum Corner Road, south of the Homochitto River. Widespread deforestation became increasingly evident as the tornado tracked east-northeast with several swaths of greater than 80% deforestation rated EF-2 for widespread snapped trunks of pine and mixed forest. The lack of well-built structures in the path of this tornado limited sampling of the peak rating of this tornado. As the tornado approached Doloroso-Rosetta Rd and the Homochitto River, the treefall pattern became cyclonic in orientation and indicative of a potential change of direction which is supported by Climavision V018 data from St. Francisville, LA. Near Old Hwy 61 Road and Perry Town Rd, barn and outbuilding structures were heavily damaged or destroyed. Almost all trees were snapped. High resolution satellite imagery also denoted numerous confluent swaths of damaging feeding into the main track from the south, indicative of subtornadic vortices and potentially a satellite tornado as it neared Old Hwy 61 Road. The tornado reached an initial peak width of 1200 yards here incorporating these feeder vortices. The tornado then continued east causing additional swaths of tree damage north of Perry Town Road before crossing the Homochitto River and back into Adams County. This tornado was continuously on the ground for approximately 81.9 miles over the span of 2 hours and 9 minutes through Adams, Wilkinson, Franklin, and Lincoln counties before concluding southwest of Monticello, MS in Lawrence County. This tornado peaked as an EF-3 east of Garden City, MS as well as near Thayer, MS in NWS Jackson's area of responsibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video documented a brief tornado in an open field around 5 miles west-southwest of Royal. The tornado was estimated to touch down around one-half mile east of 100th Avenue along 420th Street. The tornado tracked east-northeast for less than two minutes across open fields before lifting around one-quarter mile north of 420th Street one-half mile west of 120th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 20 yards based on video evidence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was observed in an open field by a storm chaser around 1 mile north of Bridgewater. The tornado was estimated to touch down around one-half mile north of the Zion Bible Church on the north edge of Bridgewater.  The tornado tracked northeast for less than one minute before it lifted southwest of the intersection of 436rd Avenue and 263rd Street. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 40 yards based on video evidence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the late evening of April 17th producing scattered wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado appeared to touch down in an open field southwest of Darrow in rural Iroquois County. It tracked northeast causing damage to trees and farm outbuildings. The peak intensity of the tornado occurred near the end of the path along the Iroquois and Newton County border, where over a dozen new wooden power poles were snapped at their base. The tornado then appeared to lift just northeast of US-24 in southwestern Newton County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported a tornado between North Hammond and Brier Hill, New York. Video  indicates the EF-0 tornado touched down in the nearby corn field and toppled an apple tree and lifted a well cover into a window of a barn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two landspout tornadoes formed south of Yoder in Goshen County during the afternoon of May 16.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This second landspout was more diffused than the one ongoing to the south, but the dust column reached up to the cloud base.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado was observed west of Highway 71 and south of County Road 44 moving due east. This tornado was initially obscured by rain and may have developed further west. The tornado began to curve towards the southeast as it underwent the occlusion process, shrinking from a stovepipe appearance to a rope as it quickly moved over farmlands and turbines. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm survey revealed a tornado developed and moved northeast across far northeast Nemaha county damaging older farm outbuidlings and barns and snapping large tree limbs.  The tornado appears to have continued into southeast Nebraska.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado moved into Juneau County from Vernon County where it intensified quickly and hit a residence at EF-3 intensity, destroying the home's above ground level. As the tornado moved east, it produced significant tree damage before weakening in intensity as it approached State Road 80, where it damaged a few more homes and several outbuildings. The tornado continued northeast, dealing intermittent tree and structural damage at EF-1 intensity along its path until it dissipated just west of Overgaard Road.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado started west of MS Highway 15 where multiple trees were uprooted and snapped near near the intersection with Kings Lane. Off of Kings Ln. there was roof damage to two single story houses, and a metal shed was destroyed. The tornado proceeded east across Highway 15, damaged a gas storage tank, destroyed another metal shed, and uprooted and snapped trees on Red Holifield Road. As the tornado continued eastward, more trees were snapped and uprooted near Township Road and Robins Road. The tornado uprooted trees as it crossed Antioch Drive and Orange Road. The tornado dissipated east of Orange Rd. Max estimated wind speeds were 110 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms occurred across Central Alabama during the late morning to early afternoon of May 22. Enough shear and instability were present to promote the development of small, low-topped supercells within a tropical environment. A few of these cells produced brief rotation, and three brief tornadoes occurred in Marengo and Tuscaloosa counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF1 tornado entered Hale County from Marengo County came to an end just past the Hale County line, along Mount Olive Road, where tree branches were broken. Damage in Hale County was of EF0 intensity.

Shingles and siding were removed from a couple of homes, a shed was destroyed, and general yard items were strewn. Perhaps the most eye-catching item was the displacement and flipping of a box truck and a pontoon boat. The tornado then crossed Highway 80 with minimal signs of damage and came to an end just past the Hale County line, along Mount Olive Road, where tree branches were broken. Maximum winds were estimated at 95 mph.

A manufactured home suffered damage to its porch and awning. Some trees were snapped and uprooted as the tornado crossed County Road 6 before dissipating as it downed trees across the road. Maximum winds were estimated at 65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Evidence of a high-end EF-1 (110mph) tornado was found in south- central Victoria County. Drone footage showed a scour track that began over farmland between Crouch Rd and HWY-185, and ended near Crouch Rd east of York Rd along with a track of debris. In between, several manufactured homes on Jared Rd, Lexie Ln, and York Rd suffered significant roof damage, broken windows, and scattered debris correlated to circulation of a tornado. One manufactured home was completely destroyed along Jared Rd. The tornado track was found to be around 1.1 miles long and a width of around 400 yards, spanning from 2:02-2:06pm CDT.

Additional EF-0 tree damage was identified on Blanchard and Smithburg roads. The tornado peaked in intensity as an EF-1 as it crossed over Harold Alford Road uprooting and snapping several trees as well as taking down wooden transmission lines. At this point, the tornado exited Pike County and entered Walthall County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 95 mph tracked across portions of northern Walthall County, near Enon, MS. This tornado began near L. L. Coon Rd where high resolution satellite imagery showed areas of damaged/displaced trees on a confined path that tracked southeast toward MS Hwy 44. The tornado strengthened to EF-1 strength as it moved into Willie Cothern Rd where it uprooted trees, lifted metal roofing off a porch, and snapped a swath of tree trunks on private property. The tornado turned more eastward as it crossed MS Hwy 583 where it damaged shingles on a church and uprooted and snapped a few trees. Minor tree damage continued eastward across New Home Church Road with plenty of tree debris across the road. The tornado then restrengthened some over inaccessible forested areas south of New Home Church Rd where patches of heavier tree damage/displacement was identified on high resolution satellite imagery. This tree damage gradually became more minor again near Hope Rd and Dee Toney Rd. Numerous small trees were leaning in a confluent pattern with large branches down near MS Hwy 27. Minor tree damage continued with uproots and large branches predominantly occurring along the damage path on Jordan, Sauls, and Dan Holmes roads. This tornado continued east-southeast into Marion County, within the NWS Jackson area of responsibility, where additional EF-0 and EF-1 tree damage was identified by ground survey. It's estimated that the tornado finally lifted near Circle Bar Road after being on the ground for approximately 13 miles and 24 minutes.

The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated peak wind of 75 mph and an estimated average width of 30 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Oklahoma during the late afternoon of April 24th, then congealed into a partially organized cluster of storms as they moved southeast across the ArkLaTex region during the evening. The storms continued to strengthen and evolved into a more organized mesoscale convective system within northwest flow aloft as they approached the local area. The MCS moved across coastal Mississippi on the early morning hours of April 25th, producing a couple of tornadoes along with areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 90 mph touched down at 30th Street and Brookwood Ave. where large branches were down on several trees. Similar damage occurred as the tornado tracked to the southeast across Pass Road and 28th Street. The tornado continued to the southeast and reached peak intensity of 90 mph near the intersection of 5th Avenue and 25th Street where a few trees were snapped. One hardwood tree was hollow inside and the other snap was very high. Numerous large branches were also removed from several trees near this intersection. The tornado then continued to the southeast crossing Gulf Avenue near 24th Street producing sporadic tree damage. The tornado then crossed the railroad just west of Hewes St. where additional large branches were removed from several trees all the way to Beach Blvd. Numerous trees were observed to have lost large branches between Roberts Ave. and Centennial Plaza on Beach Blvd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This strong EF-2 tornado began in rural portions of Olmsted County east of Viola where it damaged some farm outbuildings as it moved northeast. As the tornado approached the Wabasha County line, it strengthened and significantly damaged a farmstead, removing large sections of the roof and other portions of the home and outbuildings. It then continued northeast into Wabasha County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began near the intersection of Freeport Road and Bates Road southeast of Harrison, initially downing several tree branches at and near a small cemetery. The tornado produced additional tree damage as it tracked eastward along Roscoe Road before entering the west side of Roscoe and reaching its peak intensity as it tracked through the Hawks Point, Crystal Hills, and Oxford Commons subdivisions. There, multiple homes had portions of their roofs torn off or damaged and had sections of siding and fascia peeled off. A few homes also had their garage doors blown in, leading to parts of their garage walls getting blown out in a few cases. Numerous trees were also uprooted or damaged in these subdivisions. The tornado then continued eastward, knocking down several power poles along Gleasman Road and damaging a nearby farm outbuilding before crossing the Rock River. East of the Rock River, the tornado continued to cause extensive tree damage. Multiple additional houses sustained roof and fascia damage from the tornado as well. The tornado appeared to dissipate just as it reached the Winnebago-Boone County line. Extensive straight-line wind damage was also observed in close proximity to the tornadic circulation, particularly along its southern flank.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began along Holly Grove Circle and tracked eastward across Harrisville Braxton Road and then lifted. Along the path, multiple trees were uprooted and large tree limbs downed. The estimated maximum wind speed of this tornado was 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across SE Arkansas during the late evening hours of April 28, 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail. One of these storms produced a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief tornado occurred along County Road 498 in Ashley County. This tornado uprooted trees and caused wooden power poles to lean. The tornado crossed County Road 498 and dissipated in the field just after uprooting more trees. The tornado is rated EF-0 with winds of 85 MPH.

Hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted in the area. Some minor damage was done to a few structures on the east side of Gum Swamp Road. The tornado continued east into Covington County at Sumrall Road where additional trees were uprooted. The tornado continued northeast and ended along MS Highway 589 where it uprooted a tree and snapped some large branches. The maximum wind speed in this tornado was 105 mph.
