Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Morris County EM and local utility company provided data of damage track that begin in eastern Morris County and continued into northwestern Lyon county.  Damage occurred to tree limbs and several power poles.  One two story home had minor damage to roof.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms occurred ahead of a frontal boundary on May 22-25. However, on May 25, a mesoscale convective system developed west of the area and enhanced the low level wind field.  This resulted in two tornadoes across the tri-state area. One tornado affected the Villa Tasso area in Walton county in Florida, and the other tornado affected Houston and Henry counties in Alabama.  Both tornadoes were rated EF1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado initially touched down just north of U.S. 84 near Cowarts in Houston County, damaging trees and outbuildings. A pool screen was damaged at a home along Omussee Road, with additional tree and minor damage to homes. The tornado damaged the WDHN television station as it crossed Highway 52, breaking windows and damaging the roof. The tornado continued north-northeast downing trees and causing minor structural damage before moving into Henry County at County Road 22 and Buckhead Drive. The most severe damage was along County Road 15 where two homes were heavily damage. One home was destroyed. This home separated from the concrete foundation, slid, and then collapsed. The damage is consistent with an EF1 tornado with maximum winds of approximately 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was observed in an open field by a storm chaser around 3 miles northeast of Meriden.  The tornado was estimated to touch down just southeast of the intersection of N Avenue and 480th Street.  The tornado tracked northeast for around two minutes before it lifted east of Mill Creek.  There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 20 yards based on video evidence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and moderately unstable airmass along a cold front moving through the region  supported development of thunderstorms across southeast Louisiana late afternoon and evening of May 11th. Although weak low-level flow limited the overall severe-weather organization, locally heavy rainfall occurred in Baton Rouge metro as well as a brief tornado and associated wind damage in St. James Parish near Grand Point and Paulina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief, weak EF-0 tornado touched down in the community of Paulina, LA causing minor uplift of shingles on two homes. The tornado tracked north-northeast from Lena Street to Angelle Street at around 8 miles per hour before it was estimated to have lifted. This damage was collocated with a tight tornado vortex signature visible on TMSY doppler radar. No additional damage was identified via reports or aerial imagery. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Broad southwesterly flow aloft on the eastern side of a western CONUS trough carried several weak disturbances across the central Gulf Coast, while southeasterly low-level flow maintained deep moisture. Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi. A thunderstorm over the local marine areas produced a waterspout near the Interstate 10 Twin Span as well as severe wind gusts at other coastal locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reports a waterspout near the Twin Span.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly advancing cold front was positioned beneath strong west-southwesterly flow downstream of a broad upper-level trough with embedded shortwaves. A moist low level layer and strong instability combined with strengthening deep-layer and low-level wind shear to support discrete supercells across southwest and southern Mississippi during the late afternoon and evening. These storms produced large hail and multiple tornadoes over southwest Mississippi, one EF1 and one EF2 tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph tracked across portions of southeast Pike County and entered Walthall County near Harold Alford Road. It was  uprooting and snapping several trees as well as taking down wooden transmission lines as it traversed this area. The tornado then weakened caused EF-0 damage to trees as it crossed Brockdale Rd and the Bogue Chitto River. The end point of this tornado is estimated to be after it crossed MS Hwy 27 after it caused additional tree damage in a confluent pattern.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado formed in Byron Stewart Park, west of Cleburne, crossed onto Lake Pat Cleburne, and exited the lake on the southeast side. Tree damage was observed in the park and video evidence shows the tornado over the lake. On the southeast side of the lake along Lakeshore Dr, a small porch was damaged and overhead doors were damaged in an RV storage garage. This tornado was rated EF-0 with maximum winds of 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado continued into Wabasha County from Olmsted County where it damaged one residence, some farm outbuildings, power poles, and trees before dissipating near 230th avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down just east of MS Highway 42, tracked east, and dissipated in Covington County near MS Highway 589. Trees were damaged along Hosey Mikell, Ridgeland, Stubbs, and Willie Buckley roads. A notable increase in intensity was seen as the tornado approached and crossed Gum Swamp Road around Fairman Lane. Hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted in the area. Some minor damage was done to a few structures on the east side of Gum Swamp Road. The tornado continued east into Covington County at Sumrall Road where additional trees were uprooted. The tornado continued northeast and ended along MS Highway 589 where it uprooted a tree and snapped some large branches. The maximum wind speed in this tornado was 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began SSW of Sycamore  and tracked ENE along 5800 Rd causing EF2 damage to two houses east of the Verdigris River and north of Rd 5800. One occupant of one of the homes was unfortunately injured.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A local fire department provided a video of a brief tornado southeast of Postville. This tornado is not known to have encountered any damage indicators. Therefore, no numerical rating was able to be assigned to this tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This weak EF-0 tornado touched down approximately 3 miles northwest of Gilman and traveled northeast through mainly rural areas. Minor damage occurred to outbuildings and trees over the course of its path.

More trees were damaged along with a portion of a roof taken off a barn, a metal carport thrown and some minor roof damage to a home. The estimated maximum wind speed was 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Oklahoma during the late afternoon of April 24th, then congealed into a partially organized cluster of storms as they moved southeast across the ArkLaTex region during the evening. The storms continued to strengthen and evolved into a more organized mesoscale convective system within northwest flow aloft as they approached the local area. The MCS moved across coastal Mississippi on the early morning hours of April 25th, producing a couple of tornadoes along with areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 95 mph touched down just north of the intersection of Ohio Ave. and Polk St. in Gulfport. The tornado quickly tracked to the south causing sporadic tree damage that consisted primarily of large tree limbs being blown off of trees as tracked southward between Wisconsin Ave. and West Railroad Ave. The tornado continued south-southeast across US Hwy 49 with visible damage observed to commercial businesses in this area. Large branches and snapped trees were observed between 34th St. and 28th St. At the intersection of 28th St. and 22nd Ave. two metal buildings had their garage doors blown out as the tornado continued south-southeast. At the intersection of Pass Road and 22nd Ave. a large hardwood tree was completely uprooted. The tornado then crossed Pass Road and produced additional tree damage in the form of large branches and a few snapped trees. The snapped trees were either dead and diseased, so the windspeed was lowered to 90 mph to account for this. As the tornado crossed the railroad track, minor damage to a home in the form of a few removed shingles was observed on 3rd St. The tornado then moved offshore near the intersection of Beach Blvd. and Pratt Ave.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: This strong EF-2 tornado began on the northeast side of Stewartville resulting in damage to several homes. The tornado then moved northeast through rural areas of Olmsted County while being highly visible on MNDOT cameras and from Rochester. This tornado eventually crossed I-90, hitting a semi-trailer and injuring the occupant, before moving northwest of Simpson. A farmstead near Simpson took a direct hit from the tornado where a single-wide manufactured home was rolled and farm outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado continued northeast into a neighborhood along Marion Road where several homes were rendered uninhabitable due to a collapse of their exterior walls and roof. Numerous other residences sustained window, roof, and outbuilding damage as well. The tornado continued through this neighborhood before dissipating along Timberidge Court between Rochester and Marion. Two more individuals were also injured in this area while sheltering in their home from the tornado.

Additional tornadoes occurred as these storms traveled into Trempealeau and Jackson counties, with tree and minor structural damage along their paths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado continued from northeast Trempealeau County where it crossed Interstate 94, moving northeast into far northwest Jackson County where it caused roof damage to two residences and damaged a significant number of trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser reported the tornado was first visible in an open field west of 466th Avenue and north of 291st Street. The tornado moved slowly southeast toward a farmstead at the intersection of 466th Avenue and 291st Street where minor tree damage was reported. The primary circulation then broadened as the tornado turned more eastward and at times exhibited smaller brief vortices. Additional minor tree damage occurred before the tornado lifted in the vicinity of 291st Street and 467th Avenue. The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated peak wind of 75 mph and an estimated average path width of 50 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed in open fields near the intersection of 625 Avenue and 725 Road in Johnson county at 3:05 PM CST, and moved quickly east before entering Nemaha county. The tornado damaged many trees, flipped pivots, and destroyed at least two large farm sheds. The damage along the track was somewhat sporadic at times, and this concentrated area of tornado damage was embedded within a much broader area of 60 to 80 mph winds in the downdraft regions of the parent thunderstorm. The peak width of the tornado was determined where it traveled through a long line of trees and gave evidence to the most intense focused zone of winds being approximately 200 yards wide. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 97 mph. The tornado continued into Nemaha county before dissipating at 15:11 PM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.

The tornado then crossed US Highway 75 just northwest of the intersection with 641 Avenue, causing further tree damage and impacting a second metal outbuilding in the area. Additional tree damage occurred near Rock Creek and 642 Avenue. Maximum estimated wind speeds peaked at 100 mph.

Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary settled into the area early on July 5th. Weak low pressure developed along this front and moved into Northwest Ohio the morning of July 5th. This low pressure then remained nearly stationary through the 5th and into the 6th before weakening and exiting to the southeast later on the 6th into the 7th. The front and low pressure combined with a weak trough aloft to encourage periods of showers and thunderstorms from the 5th through the 6th. A warm and very humid airmass combined with weak steering flow to support slow-moving thunderstorms with torrential rainfall rates. There were a few different waves of thunderstorms with heavy rain. An initial batch of thunderstorms tracked across northern Ohio during the morning and early afternoon of the 5th, bringing flash flooding and severe weather to the Youngstown area. An EF-1 tornado and macroburst caused extensive wind damage across Mahoning County, leading to widespread power outages and a state of emergency declaration. Additional thunderstorms the evening of the 5th brought flash flooding across North Central Ohio. Lake enhanced showers and thunderstorms developed over Lake Erie overnight July 5th into the 6th, with east-northeast winds pushing this activity towards the western lakeshore. The most notable impacts came on Kelleys Island, where 10 to 15 inches of rain fell over a several hour period and led to significant flash flooding during the early morning hours of the 6th. Additional flooding occurred later in the morning and into the afternoon on the mainland from just south of Toledo to the Port Clinton area, with more storms developing during the afternoon and causing flash flooding east of Cleveland in parts of Lake and Geauga Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Storm Survey team has determined that a very short-lived EF-1 tornado with winds of 95 mph occurred in Canfield Township on July 5, 2026. The tornado formed in the vicinity of Mellinger Road, where the tops of trees were shredded and thrown onto nearby residences. The tornado continued southeast across US 62, where the tornado toppled more trees and snapped several at their bases with some slight convergent motion. One large tree fell onto a residence severely damaging the home. The tornado continued southeast toward Messerly Road where more tree tops were shredded before the tornado cycled out. This short-lived EF-1 tornado had estimated maximum wind gusts of 95 mph in northeast Canfield Township and was on the ground for about a minute.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 21st, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Ohio Valley along a cold front. The storms and the cold front pushed from northwest to southeast across southern Indiana and central Kentucky as an amplified mid- and upper-level trough pivoted across the eastern United States. Along and south of the cold front, a hot and humid environment was present, with temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s and dewpoint temperatures in the mid-to-upper 70s. The heat and humidity near the surface combined with cooling temperatures aloft resulted in a very unstable environment, with between 3500 and 4500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE observed. What made this setup uniquely potent was abnormally strong wind shear thanks to 40-50 knots of mid-level west-northwesterly flow. This resulted in well-organized, severe convection across the region, with a mixture of supercells, multicell clusters, and bowing segments observed across the area. While all severe hazard types were observed, damaging winds and tornadoes were the primary impact, with several swaths of straight-line wind damage and spin-up tornadoes observed. The most potent storm of the event was a supercell which tracked across Grayson, Hart, and Metcalfe County, producing three separate tornadoes, including a 21 mile-long EF-2 which went from Nolin River Lake to near the Hart and Barren County line. While storms moved at a fairly good clip to the southeast, precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches resulted in efficient rainfall production in some areas, with several instances of flash flooding observed across the area.

A humid, unstable environment was present throughout this time period with dew point temperatures in the mid 70s and precipitable water values near or exceeding 2 inches. On top of this, relatively weak steering flow in the mid-levels of the atmosphere lead to slow movement of showers and thunderstorms which developed, resulting in localized heavy rainfall amounts and flash flooding. Scattered flash flooding occurred across central Kentucky over the four day period, with severe weather impacts mainly being limited to isolated downbursts from hydrometeor loading in otherwise disorganized cells. However, by the 9th, the ingestion of the cutoff low into broader troughing did provide for slightly stronger wind shear and better storm organization. With a seasonably humid and unstable environment remaining in place, this stronger wind shear did promote a bit more coverage of strong to severe storms, with a couple wind damage reports and a spin-up tornado being observed during the evening and early nighttime hours on July 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 21st, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Ohio Valley along a cold front. The storms and the cold front pushed from northwest to southeast across southern Indiana and central Kentucky as an amplified mid- and upper-level trough pivoted across the eastern United States. Along and south of the cold front, a hot and humid environment was present, with temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s and dewpoint temperatures in the mid-to-upper 70s. The heat and humidity near the surface combined with cooling temperatures aloft resulted in a very unstable environment, with between 3500 and 4500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE observed. What made this setup uniquely potent was abnormally strong wind shear thanks to 40-50 knots of mid-level west-northwesterly flow. This resulted in well-organized, severe convection across the region, with a mixture of supercells, multicell clusters, and bowing segments observed across the area. While all severe hazard types were observed, damaging winds and tornadoes were the primary impact, with several swaths of straight-line wind damage and spin-up tornadoes observed. The most potent storm of the event was a supercell which tracked across Grayson, Hart, and Metcalfe County, producing three separate tornadoes, including a 21 mile-long EF-2 which went from Nolin River Lake to near the Hart and Barren County line. While storms moved at a fairly good clip to the southeast, precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches resulted in efficient rainfall production in some areas, with several instances of flash flooding observed across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado crossed from Casey County into Lincoln County and began weakening as it moved towards Black Pike west of Hustonville. Power poles were snapped along with additional large tree limbs snapped with estimated winds of 85 mph, or a high end EF-0. |Shortly after, the tornado lifted and no other tornadic damage was observed.

Storms congealed and moved southeast through the area in broken line segments producing swaths of wind damage and a couple embedded tornadoes. Training of storms lead to isolated instances of flash flooding as well.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief small tornado occurred on the western edge of Wayne County in the South Canaan vicinity. A heavy shower started exhibiting loose rotation while crossing the Archbald Mountain ridge. As the shower dropped in elevation, rotation quickly tightened to spin up a short-lived EF0 tornado. So oddly enough, this storm produced a tornado before lightning. It took out several well-established apple trees in an orchard, while causing siding and soffit damage to a couple houses as well as destroying a hunter shed. Smaller branches were deposited in a convergent path across a field, and a chair was even lofted nearly a quarter of a mile. The tornado lost some intensity while tracking over and then past Lake Quinn, before falling apart shortly after Easton Turnpike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pictures and video of damage, combined with radar data, indicate a brief EF-1 tornado occurred in the Uvalde Estates subdivision. The tornado occurred along Windmill Road, west of White Trail Drive. A wood power pole was snapped and another was leaning. Tree damage was also observed. While unable to verify, it is possible the tornado was on the ground longer, extending farther south and north of Windmill Road. Time was estimated from radar. The damage was rated as EF-1 with maximum wind speeds of 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front stationed across central Pennsylvania allowed for a lifting mechanism for showers and storms during the morning and afternoon hours of July 5, 2026. Showers and isolated thunderstorms began to develop across portions of western and central Pennsylvaia during the late morning hours and began to exhibit slow forward motion and instances of training. This continued into the afternoon and evening hours, where heavy rainfall persisted over Tyrone in Blair County for upwards of an hour. This prompted considerable flash flooding in the borough, with multiple homes being flooded and some roadways taking on between two and three feet of water. There were also two children that were rescued from flood waters near the paper mill in Tyrone due to the flooding. Given the unstable airmass, thunderstorms continued to grow upscale throughout the afternoon and evening hours, producing multiple instances of tree damage across Centre, Mifflin and Franklin Counties. As storms shifted eastward, favorable low-level shear allowed for some storms to form into a line with some areas of rotation, one of which prompted the Lambs Gap EF-1 Tornado in Perry County. This line continued to move eastward and produced multiple instances of wind damage and flash flooding in Cumberland, Dauphin, and Lancaster Counties throughout the evening before shifting east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 100 mph, a path length of 0.55 miles, and a maximum width of 300 yards occurred along Lamb's Gap Road in Perry County on July 5, 2026. The tornado path started just north of Evergreen Drive, and traveled south-southwest breaking off and uprooting numerous trees. The most concentrated damage was along Lamb's Gap Road near the edge of the State Game Lands. The damage seemed to end less than 50 yards to the southwest of Lamb's Gap Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of weakening thunderstorms moved into the northeast Gerogia mountains from the north during the evening. The storms produced a weak tornado in the far northern part of the county and a small area of damaging winds in the Clarkesville area.

Several areas of downed trees were observed along Goshen Mountain Road south towards Highway 356 near the intersection of Highway 197. It is possible additional trees were downed to the north of the start of the observed path, but inaccessible roads prevented determining the actual start point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A volatile air mass with up to 3000-4000+ J/kg MLCAPE and 30 to 40 knots of deep layer shear developed by early afternoon over south central and parts of southeast South Dakota. Moisture pooled near a convectively enhanced outflow boundary from overnight convection, and stronger heating toward south central South Dakota broke the cap by early afternoon near enhanced convergence near Chamberlain. Initial cells were very slow moving and isolated, leading to longer-lived intense updrafts. By late afternoon, storms evolved into a broken linear structure as convection entered southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado was witnessed by several storm chasers as it developed just north of 229th Street around 4 miles northeast of Spring Valley Colony. The tornado tracked northeast in an open area along a creek for around one-half mile before it crossed South Dakota Highway 34. The tornado continued northeast for a couple more minutes before it crossed 368th Avenue.  The tornado dissipated about a minute later just east of the end of 227th Street. The tornado could not be rated (EFU) due to a lack of damage indicators. The average path width based on video was around 20 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along and out ahead of an approaching cold front in two rounds. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 21st, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Ohio Valley along a cold front. The storms and the cold front pushed from northwest to southeast across southern Indiana and central Kentucky as an amplified mid- and upper-level trough pivoted across the eastern United States. Along and south of the cold front, a hot and humid environment was present, with temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s and dewpoint temperatures in the mid-to-upper 70s. The heat and humidity near the surface combined with cooling temperatures aloft resulted in a very unstable environment, with between 3500 and 4500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE observed. What made this setup uniquely potent was abnormally strong wind shear thanks to 40-50 knots of mid-level west-northwesterly flow. This resulted in well-organized, severe convection across the region, with a mixture of supercells, multicell clusters, and bowing segments observed across the area. While all severe hazard types were observed, damaging winds and tornadoes were the primary impact, with several swaths of straight-line wind damage and spin-up tornadoes observed. The most potent storm of the event was a supercell which tracked across Grayson, Hart, and Metcalfe County, producing three separate tornadoes, including a 21 mile-long EF-2 which went from Nolin River Lake to near the Hart and Barren County line. While storms moved at a fairly good clip to the southeast, precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches resulted in efficient rainfall production in some areas, with several instances of flash flooding observed across the area.

The tornado continued southward across the Cumberland|Parkway. The most widespread damage was along Columbia Road, where large limbs were toppled on to some homes and some large trees were uprooted. The tornado continued its path through a residence along Breeding Road, where it likely lifted just south of Breeding Road.

The tornado crossed Oquaga Creek and caused more EF-1 level damage on Farnham Road and Old Plank Road. The damage mainly consisted of numerous downed trees, including a tree that fell onto a car. A home was damaged when the metal skirting was blown out from underneath it on Farnham Road. The tornado continued tracking southeast over a hill and paralleled Old Plank Road and Old Route 17 where it caused lighter sporadic tree damage at an EF-0 level. The weak tornado continued south and east, crossing State Route 17 just west of exit 83. It continued south and east, likely causing sporadic damage as it crossed over the inaccessible Whittacker Swamp State Forest. There was visible damage of numerous trees down and snapped along the hillside just west of River Road and State Highway 17. The weak tornado continued on, to the south and east causing light damage as it moved through the town of Hale Eddy, NY. Tornado briefly tracked into Wayne County PA with additional tree damage across the Delaware River along Penn York Road. The tornado crossed NY Route 17 again and moved across the town of Hancock, causing significant tree damage at the Hancock Golf Course. The tornado then crossed county highway 268 and the East Branch of the Delaware River. It restrengthened to EF-1 and caused significant tree damage mainly along the south bank of the river, along with some damage to out buildings and porches of residences. The tornado lifted just southeast of Peas Eddy Road as it moved up the hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Comparison of high resolution satellite imagery taken on June 27 and July 27 indicates a narrow swath of vegetation damage near and along Shields Ranch/Phillips Rd and Ranch Creek southeast of Camp Wood. The damage swath was consistent and aligned with a weak tornadic debris signature observed on the morning of July 16 from the KDFX WSR-88D. Intermittent tree damage may have occurred farther to the northwest past the northwestern terminus of the defined satellite-observed data swath. This satellite analysis was corroborated with a report of damaged, broken, and mangled live oak canopy along the path at Shield Ranch. The EF0 intensity was assessed based on this report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Initial shower and thunderstorm coverage during the morning hours of July 18, 2026 moved east of the region and allowed for ample recovery with respect to instability across the region during the late morning and early afternoon hours. The remnants of a MCS that tracked across Ohio and western Pennsylvania continued into northern Somerset County during the morning hours and produced multiple instances of tree damage as it continued into northern Bedford County in the early afternoon hours. At the same time, thunderstorm development across northwestern Pennsylvania began to rapidly show upscale growth within a strongly sheared and unstable environment, allowing for multiple instances of tree damage in Warren County. Storms began to quickly show signs of rotation as they moved further southeast into Elk County and produced wind damage, but no convergent patterns in damage were found. As these storms continues southeastward with continued rotation, a tornado occurred in northern Centre County and multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Clinton County. In the late afternoon hours, additional rotating cells came from western Pennsylvania, spawning an EF-2 tornado in Somerset County where widespread tree damage was observed. These cells also spawned three tornadoes, with an EF-1 in Clearfield County, an EF-2 in Huntingdon County, and an EF-0 in Blair County. Wind damage continues to be observed from these storms through the Lower Susquehanna Valley, mainly in the form of tree damage. Multiple rounds of storms in Clearfield and Somerset Counties also resulted in isolated instances of flash flooding on roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-2 tornado with estimated peak winds of 125 mph, a path length of 0.72 miles, and a maximum width of 100 yards occurred in Jenner Township on July 18, 2026. The tornado began west of the Conemaugh Township Reservoir where minor damage to trees was noted. The tornado began to strengthen as it moved to the east-southeast and hundreds of trees were snapped or uprooted, with virtually no trees remaining standing in a quarter-mile swath just to the west of the reservoir. Damage to trees continued as the tornado moved along Ferndale Drive before coming to an end near Bens Creek.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado initially began about five miles southeast of Ghent along Kentucky State Route 47 near and northwest of Interstate 71, where some large branches were downed. Additionally, a couple of large trees were downed in the same area. The tornado then continued southeast toward the Carroll/Gallatin County line. The tornado entered Gallatin County at 1414EST and continued southeast toward the Owen County line, crossing into Owen County at 1415EST. The tornado fully crossed into Grant County at approximately 1445EST, where it took a more eastward turn. The tornado finally dissipated in Grant County at 1526EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist, weakly forced summertime environment persisted across southeast Louisiana on July 1st as the upper ridge shifted slightly northeast of the region and the previous night's easterly disturbance increased moisture across the area. Scattered convection developed along coastal and mesoscale boundaries by midday. A waterspout developed over the marsh and coastal waters near Hopedale and Delacroix.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed several pictures of a waterspout in the marshes near Hopedale and Delacroix.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms tracked north to south through the Devils Lake Basin during the evening hours producing damaging winds and several weak tornadoes. One tornado was EF-0 southwest of Maddock, ND in Benson County. The other did not have a damage indicator that could be rated as it passed into far northwest Benson County from Pierce County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of thin tornado in open field northwest of Knox from local fire department and trained spotters. This matches location of track apparent on Sentinel satellite. Based on Sentinel satellite the tornado touched down in Pierce County and tracked to the southeast into Benson County before lifting. There currently known damage indicators along this track in Benson County that can be used for rating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, bringing a warm and humid airmass to the Ohio Valley. Thunderstorms developed in this airmass ahead of a cold front, bringing heavy rainfall and severe weather to the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred at a single family residence off of Henry Road, where a hardwood tree was snapped and downed onto the roof of the home. Additionally, the field adjacent to the home had flattened cornstalks, with minor tree damage observed across the street. More flattened cornstalks were observed in a field near the intersection of Henry Road and State Highway 729. More significant damage occurred along Larrick Road, where several properties sustained tree damage. One property in particular had six trees that were either uprooted or snapped at the base. The last observed damage occurred on Larrick Road, where a tree was uprooted and additional cornstalks were partially flattened. The tornado is believed to have dissipated beyond this point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Onshore flow in place supported sufficient moisture influx resulting in scattered morning showers and thunderstorms over the coastal waters on July 2nd. With little organized large-scale forcing and generally light winds, localized convergence beneath developing showers provided a favorable environment for waterspouts. A weak waterspout was observed near South Pass followed by another one over Lake Borgne south of Lake Catherine in the morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report with photos showing a weak waterspout near South pass from a passing storm.

The tornado continued producing tree damage until it ended near Chicago Heights-Glenwood Road, just east of Thorn Creek.
